title: Neurogenic pain
description: Facial and oral pain of neurogenic, vascular, or central origin — the differentials for the toothache that doesn't behave like a toothache.

problems.description: Lightning-shock pain on one side of the face triggered by touching a specific spot — shaving, eating, cold air — lasting only seconds.
problems.etiology: The most common neurological cause of facial pain. Thought to be a sensory form of epilepsy, although some cases are due to vascular pressure or nerve demyelination intracranially [1]. Patients under 50 presenting with cranial nerve neuralgia require full neurological examination and MRI, as these may be the presenting symptoms of an intracranial neoplasm, skull base metastases, HIV, syphilis, or multiple sclerosis [2].
problems.presentation: Excruciating paroxysmal shooting 'electric shock' type of pain of rapid onset and short duration (few seconds to less than 2 minutes), affecting one side of the face in the distribution of the trigeminal nerve [1]. Often stimulated by touching a trigger point in the distribution of the trigeminal nerve — patients may refuse to shave or wash the area [1]. Strangely, they are rarely woken by it [1]. In the early stages there may be a period of prodromal pain not conforming to the classical description [1].
problems.results: Patients often have multiple extractions in an attempt to relieve the symptoms before the correct diagnosis is reached [1]. Diagnosis is by the history alone; no objective signs are present. Carbamazepine is useful both therapeutically and diagnostically, with an 80% response rate [1].
problems.definingCharacteristics: The defining feature that separates this from every other neuropain condition is the trigger zone: a small patch of facial skin or mucosa where light, innocuous contact (touch, airflow, chewing) reliably fires a paroxysmal electric-shock burst lasting only seconds. No other condition in this origin has a discrete contact trigger zone. Cluster headache pain is continuous over 30–60 minutes, not triggered by touch. Atypical odontalgia is a constant deep ache without paroxysms. Post-herpetic neuralgia burns continuously without a touch trigger.
problems.treatment: Injection of LA can break pain cycles and be useful diagnostically [1]. Other useful drugs are gabapentin and pregabalin [1]. Surgical management includes peripheral treatments such as cryotherapy, chemical destruction of nerve (alcohol/phenol), or radiofrequency ablation and central neurosurgical procedures such as microvascular decompression, glycerol or radiofrequency rhizotomy, or gamma knife radiosurgery [1].
problems.prognosis: Carbamazepine achieves an 80% response rate and is the first-line agent [1]. Surgical options carry good long-term results in refractory cases. The condition has a tendency to relapse over years; a small proportion of cases reflect underlying demyelinating disease or intracranial pathology and carry the prognosis of those diagnoses [2].

citations.quote: This is the most common neurological cause of facial pain, it is an excruciating condition affecting mainly the >50s, F > M. It presents as a paroxysmal shooting 'electric shock' type of pain of rapid onset and short duration (few seconds to less than 2min), affecting one side of the face in the distribution of the trigeminal nerve. It is often stimulated by touching a trigger point in the distribution of the trigeminal nerve. Patients may refuse to shave or wash the area which stimulates the pain although, strangely, they are rarely woken by it. In the early stages of the disease there may be a period of prodromal pain not conforming to the classical description and it may be difficult to arrive at a ∆; patients often have multiple extractions in an attempt to relieve the symptoms. It is thought to be a sensory form of epilepsy, although some cases are due to vascular pressure or nerve demyelination intracranially. ∆ is by the history, and carbamazepine is useful both therapeutically and diagnostically, with an 80% response rate. Injection of LA can break pain cycles and be useful diagnostically. Other useful drugs are gabapentin and pregabalin. Surgical management includes peripheral Rxs such as cryotherapy, chemical destruction of nerve (alcohol/phenol), or radiofrequency ablation and central neurosurgical procedures such as microvascular decompression, glycerol or radiofrequency rhizotomy, or gamma knife radiosurgery.

Patients under the age of 50yrs presenting with symptoms of cranial nerve neuralgia require full neurological examination and a MRI scan, as these may be the presenting symptoms of an intracranial neoplasm, skull base metastases, HIV, syphilis, or multiple sclerosis. Bilateral neuralgic symptoms indicate demyelination until proven otherwise.

problems.description: Persistent burning pain across one side of the face following a blistering skin rash, continuing long after the skin has healed.
problems.etiology: Varicella zoster virus (HZV) is a neurogenic DNA virus which causes shingles as a reactivation, the virus staying in the dorsal root ganglion of a peripheral nerve or the trigeminal ganglion [1]. Post-herpetic neuralgia follows acute shingles in up to 15% of cases [2]. Shingles is commoner in the immunocompromised, alcoholics, and elderly people [1].
problems.presentation: Shingles presents as pre-eruption pain followed by development of painful vesicles on skin or oral mucosa, confined to the distribution of a nerve, always unilateral, never crossing the midline [1]. Facial or oral lesions arise in the area supplied by branches of the trigeminal nerve [1]. After the vesicles clear in 2–4 weeks, severe post-herpetic neuralgia may continue for years [2]. The residual pain is typically described as persistent burning or aching in the affected dermatome.
problems.results: Aggressive early treatment of shingles with aciclovir (within 3 days of first vesicle) reduces the incidence and severity of post-herpetic neuralgia in immunocompromised patients [2]. Once established, post-herpetic neuralgia is very difficult to treat. Urgent referral to an ophthalmologist is required if the eye is involved, as there is a risk of corneal ulceration and visual loss [2].
problems.definingCharacteristics: Separation from other neuropain entries rests on the sequence: a preceding vesicular rash in a trigeminal dermatome is required for this diagnosis. No touch trigger fires a paroxysm (distinguishing it from trigeminal neuralgia). The pain is not localised to a tooth site or edentulous alveolus (distinguishing it from atypical odontalgia). There are no autonomic symptoms and no nocturnal clustering (distinguishing it from cluster headache). The dermatomal scar or residual skin changes are often visible on examination.
problems.treatment: Symptomatic relief is the mainstay. There is some evidence that aggressive early treatment of shingles with aciclovir (within 3 days of first vesicle) reduces the incidence and severity of post-herpetic neuralgia in immunocompromised patients [2]. For established post-herpetic neuralgia, tricyclic antidepressants, gabapentin, and pregabalin are used; specialist pain team involvement is often necessary.
problems.prognosis: Post-herpetic neuralgia may continue for years after the acute episode [2]. It is recognised as one of the most treatment-resistant chronic pain states in dental and medical practice. Prognosis for complete resolution is poor once established; partial symptom control is the realistic goal.

citations.quote: Shingles is commoner in the immunocompromised, alcoholics, and elderly people. It is confined to the distribution of a nerve, the virus staying either in the dorsal root ganglion of a peripheral nerve or the trigeminal ganglion. It always presents as a unilateral lesion, never crossing the midline. Facial or oral lesions may arise in the area supplied by the branches of the trigeminal nerve.

∆: pre-eruption pain, followed by development of painful vesicles on skin or oral mucosa, which rupture to give ulcers or crusting skin wounds, in the distribution outlined previously. These usually clear in 2–4 weeks, with scarring and pigmentations and is often followed by severe post-herpetic neuralgia (up to 15%) which may continue for years. Rx: symptomatic relief for chickenpox. There is some evidence to suggest that aggressive early Rx of shingles with aciclovir (within 3 days of first vesicle) ↓ the incidence and severity of post-herpetic neuralgia in immunocompromised patients. Urgent referral to an ophthalmologist is required if the eye is involved as there is a risk of corneal ulceration and visual loss.

problems.description: Sudden onset of one-sided facial drooping, inability to close the eye or smile, often preceded by pain around the ear.
problems.etiology: Caused by inflammation of cranial nerve VII in the stylomastoid canal [1]. Lower motor neurone paralysis of the facial nerve — distinguishable from upper motor neurone stroke because the forehead has a degree of bilateral innervation and is relatively spared in upper motor neurone lesions [2]. Bell's palsy is listed among the neurological causes of facial paralysis alongside Ramsay Hunt syndrome, Guillain-Barré syndrome, trauma, and infiltration by malignant tumours [3].
problems.presentation: Although the main symptom is facial paralysis, pain in or around the ear, often radiating to the jaw, precedes or develops at the same time in approximately 50% of cases [1]. The facial nerve is motor to the muscles of facial expression; testing involves having the patient raise their eyebrows, screw their eyes shut, whistle, smile, and show their teeth [2]. Taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue (chorda tympani) may also be affected [2].
problems.results: Steroids improve the chance for full recovery if treatment is started early (within 3 days of onset) [1]. If no treatment is given, 20% of patients will not completely recover [1]. The cornea must be protected with an eye pad due to inability to close the eye [1]. Combining aciclovir with steroid or aciclovir alone does not appear to improve recovery over steroid alone [1].
problems.definingCharacteristics: Bell's palsy is the only condition in this origin presenting primarily as a motor deficit rather than pain. The facial droop with inability to close the eye, whistle, or smile is pathognomonic — no other neuropain entry produces lower motor neurone facial paralysis. The ear pain that often accompanies it can mislead toward dental diagnosis, but the motor signs resolve the differential immediately. Ramsay Hunt syndrome is distinguished by associated herpetic vesicles in the external auditory meatus.
problems.treatment: Steroids improve the chance for full recovery if treatment is started early (within 3 days of onset) [1]. Protect the cornea with an eye pad [1]. Combining aciclovir with steroid or aciclovir alone does not appear to improve recovery over steroid alone [1].
problems.prognosis: If treated promptly with steroids, the majority recover fully. Without treatment, 20% of patients will not completely recover [1]. Residual facial weakness, synkinesis, or incomplete eye closure may persist in those who do not recover fully.

citations.quote: Caused by inflammation of cranial nerve VII in the stylomastoid canal. Although the main symptom is facial paralysis, pain in or around the ear, often radiating to the jaw, precedes or develops at the same time in ~50% of cases. Rx: steroids improve chance for full recovery if Rx early (within 3 days of onset). If no Rx, 20% of patients will not completely recover. Protect cornea with eye pad. Combining aciclovir with steroid or aciclovir alone does not appear to improve recovery over steroid alone.

The facial nerve is motor to the muscles of facial expression and stapedius, secretomotor to the submandibular and sublingual salivary glands, and relays taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue via the chorda tympani. It is tested by having the patient raise their eyebrows, screw their eyes shut, whistle, smile, and show their teeth. Upper and lower motor neurone lesions can be distinguished because the forehead has a degree of bilateral innervation and is relatively spared in upper motor neurone lesions.

Lower motor neurone paralysis can be caused by Bell's palsy, trauma, infiltration by malignant tumours, Ramsay Hunt syndrome, or Guillain–Barré syndrome (post-viral polyneuritis, may even appear to be bilateral).

problems.description: Constant deep aching or burning pain at a tooth or extraction site that persists or worsens despite technically sound dental treatment.
problems.etiology: Diagnosis is of exclusion. Constitutes a large proportion of patients presenting with facial pain. Mostly middle-aged women (70%) [1]. Symptoms are unrelated to the anatomical distribution of nerves or any known pathological process, and these patients have often been through a number of specialist disciplines in an attempt to establish a diagnosis [1]. There may be a florid psychiatric history or undiagnosed depression (50% are depressed or hypochondriacal) [1].
problems.presentation: Pain is described as deep, constant ache or burning [1]. Classically there are no relieving or exacerbating factors [1]. Sleeping and eating are not obviously disturbed, despite continuous unbearable pain [1]. Most analgesics are said to be unhelpful, although many will not have tried adequate analgesia [1]. The pain persists after or is not relieved by extraction, root canal treatment, or other definitive dental procedures. No objective signs are demonstrable and all investigations are essentially normal [1].
problems.results: Pointers to a psychogenic aetiology include imprecise localisation, pain that crosses the midline, frequently moves to another site or is 'all over the place', and bizarre or grossly exaggerated descriptions [1]. No objective signs are demonstrable and all investigations are essentially normal [1]. After exclusion of any possible organic cause, tricyclic antidepressants, gabapentin, or pregabalin can help. The specialist pain team with access to psychological input may be of help [1].
problems.definingCharacteristics: The defining feature is onset or persistence at a dental treatment site (extraction socket, root-treated tooth, or sound tooth) where no organic pathology is found and treatment has made no difference or has worsened the pain — the opposite of the expected clinical course. No touch trigger fires a paroxysm (contrast trigeminal neuralgia). No vesicular prodrome (contrast post-herpetic neuralgia). No autonomic features or nocturnal periodicity (contrast cluster headache). No motor deficit (contrast Bell's palsy). The dental treatment context and the diagnosis-of-exclusion process are the discriminators.
problems.treatment: After exclusion of any possible organic cause, tricyclic antidepressants, gabapentin, or pregabalin can help [1]. The specialist pain team with access to psychological input may be of help [1]. Further dental intervention is contraindicated and typically worsens the condition.
problems.prognosis: Prognosis is guarded. The condition tends to be chronic and resistant to conventional analgesia [1]. Tricyclics and gabapentinoids provide partial relief in some patients. Psychological input improves outcomes. Repeated dental surgical intervention does not help and reinforces the pain behaviour.

citations.quote: Diagnosis is of exclusion. Constitutes a large proportion of patients presenting with facial pain. Mostly middle aged women (70%). Classically, their symptoms are unrelated to anatomical distribution of nerves or any known pathological process, and these patients have often been through a number of specialist disciplines in an attempt to establish a ∆. This ∆ tends to be used as a catch-all for a large group of patients, with the connecting underlying supposition that the pain is of psychogenic origin. There may be a florid psychiatric history or undiagnosed depression (50% are depressed or hypochondriacal). Pointers to a psychogenic aetiology include imprecise localization, crosses midline, often bilateral pain, frequently moves to another site or 'all over the place'. Bizarre or grossly exaggerated descriptions of pain. Pain is described as deep, constant ache or burning and there are no relieving or exacerbating factors. Sleeping and eating are not obviously disturbed, despite continuous unbearable pain. Most analgesics are said to be unhelpful, although many will not have tried adequate analgesia. No objective signs are demonstrable and all investigations are essentially normal. After exclusion of any possible organic cause, tricyclic antidepressants, gabapentin, or pregabalin can help. The specialist pain team with access to psychological input may be of help.

problems.description: Severe boring pain around one eye, lasting 30–60 minutes, recurring nightly in clusters — with a watering eye and blocked nostril on the same side.
problems.etiology: Has a similar aetiology to migraine but with a different clinical presentation [1]. Periodic attacks of severe, unilateral pain; most sufferers describe alcohol intolerance [1]. The condition can mimic acute dental pain and leads patients to seek dental assessment before the neurological diagnosis is made.
problems.presentation: Periodic attacks of severe, unilateral pain, boring or burning in character, lasting 30–60 minutes, located around the eye; commonly associated with autonomic symptoms such as watering of the eye on the affected side, congestion of the conjunctiva, and nasal discharge [1]. Attacks often occur at a particular time of night ('alarm clock wakening'), and tend to be closely concentrated over a period of time, followed by a longer period of remission [1]. Most sufferers describe alcohol intolerance [1].
problems.results: Oxygen inhalation in an acute attack is both effective and diagnostic [1]. NSAIDs, ergotamine or sumatriptan, and intranasal lidocaine are also used acutely [1]. Pizotifen is used prophylactically [1]. The nocturnal periodicity and clustering pattern, combined with unilateral autonomic features, distinguish this from dental pain.
problems.definingCharacteristics: Three features simultaneously are pathognomonic and absent in every other entry in this origin: (1) strict nocturnal periodicity with an 'alarm clock' pattern, (2) autonomic symptoms ipsilateral to the pain (lacrimation, conjunctival injection, nasal congestion), and (3) clustering periods with remission intervals. Trigeminal neuralgia is seconds-long and touch-triggered. Post-herpetic neuralgia follows a rash. Atypical odontalgia is constant without periodicity. Bell's palsy is a motor deficit. IAN injury follows surgery. None of the others have autonomic features or clock-like recurrence.
problems.treatment: O2 inhalation (effectiveness in acute attack is diagnostic), NSAIDs, ergotamine or sumatriptan, intranasal lidocaine [1]. Pizotifen is used prophylactically [1].
problems.prognosis: Attacks resolve spontaneously within cluster periods, followed by remission [1]. Long-term prognosis is variable; some patients have episodic clusters for decades. The condition is non-destructive but severely disabling during active periods. Prophylactic pizotifen reduces attack frequency.

citations.quote: This has a similar aetiology to migraine but with a different clinical presentation: periodic attacks of severe, unilateral pain, boring or burning in character, lasting 30–60min, located around the eye; commonly associated with autonomic symptoms such as watering of eye on affected side, congestion of conjunctiva, and nasal discharge. Attacks often occur at a particular time of night (early morning 'alarm clock wakening'), and tend to be closely concentrated over a period of time, followed by a longer period of remission. Most sufferers describe alcohol intolerance. Rx: O2 inhalation (effectiveness in acute attack is diagnostic), NSAIDs, ergotamine or sumatriptan, intranasal lidocaine. Pizotifen is used prophylactically.

problems.description: Numbness, tingling, or altered sensation of the lip, chin, or tongue following surgical removal of a lower wisdom tooth.
problems.conditionName: Inferior alveolar, lingual, or mental nerve injury following lower third molar extraction
problems.etiology: The inferior alveolar nerve, mental nerve, and lingual nerve are all at risk during lower third molar surgery [1]. Radiographic signs of increased risk of nerve damage include: proximity to nerve canal, narrowing or diversion of canal, darkening of root/interrupting white lines of canal, interruption of lamina dura, and juxta-apical area [2]. Reported rates for conventional surgical removal are 8% temporary and 3.6% permanent altered sensation [3].
problems.presentation: Paraesthesia or anaesthesia in the distribution of the inferior alveolar nerve (lower lip and chin) or lingual nerve (anterior tongue, floor of mouth), presenting immediately post-operatively or within the first 24–48 hours. The patient reports numbness, tingling, burning, or electric-shock sensations in the affected distribution. Mental nerve compression by a denture flange following alveolar resorption is a separate variant producing a sensation like an electric shock but with a background ache which increases during the day and decreases overnight [4].
problems.results: The majority of cases represent neurapraxia (nerve compression without axonal disruption) and recover spontaneously over weeks to months. Permanent deficit (neurotmesis) occurs in a minority — reported permanent rate approximately 3.6% for conventional surgical removal [3]. Coronectomy (intentional crown removal with root retention) was introduced specifically to reduce this risk when roots are radiographically assessed as closely involved with the ID canal [3].
problems.definingCharacteristics: The discriminating feature within this origin is the surgical trigger: altered sensation follows a specific operative event (third molar extraction or other lower jaw surgery), is dermatomal in distribution, and begins in the immediate post-operative period. No other condition in this origin has this onset pattern. Trigeminal neuralgia is paroxysmal and touch-triggered, not post-surgical numbness. Post-herpetic neuralgia follows a vesicular rash. Atypical odontalgia is pain at a dental site, not dermatomal sensory loss. Bell's palsy is a motor deficit of cranial nerve VII, not a sensory deficit of cranial nerve V.
problems.treatment: Warn the patient before surgery about the possibility of damage to the ID and lingual nerves [5]. If roots are radiographically assessed as closely involved with the ID canal, coronectomy (removal of the crown, deliberate retention of roots) is an alternative to complete removal [3]. For established nerve injury, watchful waiting is appropriate for the first 3 months as most are neurapraxia and recover. Microsurgical nerve repair may be considered for persistent neurotmesis. There is good evidence to suggest that manipulation from the lingual aspect results in unnecessary lingual nerve morbidity — bone and tooth removal should be from a buccal approach [6].
problems.prognosis: Reported rates for conventional surgical removal are 8% temporary, and 3.6% permanent [3]. Coronectomy compares favourably to surgical removal of lower wisdom teeth in terms of altered sensation [3]. Patients with identified radiographic high-risk signs who undergo coronectomy have a lower incidence of permanent deficit, as the nerve was likely closely involved with the root in those cases [3].

citations.quote: It is crucial that key anatomical structures are identified by the surgeon prior to and during implant placement to ensure injuries (e.g. laceration, section, or compression) are avoided where possible. Moderate- to high-risk structures include the inferior alveolar nerve, mental nerve, lingual nerve, and sublingual/submental arteries.

Radiographic signs of ↑ risk of nerve damage include: Proximity to nerve canal. Narrowing or diversion of canal. Darkening of root/interrupting white lines of canal. Interruption of lamina dura. Juxta-apical area.

Coronectomy compares favourably to surgical removal of lower wisdom teeth in terms of altered sensation: reported rates for conventional surgical removal are 8% temporary, and 3.6% permanent (personal rates vary). There is a similar incidence of dry socket (10–12%).

Mental nerve compression by a denture flange following alveolar resorption is a common problem, producing a sensation like an electric shock but with a background ache which ↑ during the day and ↓ overnight.
Warn the patient about pain, trismus, swelling, and the possibility of damage to the ID and lingual nerves.
There is now good evidence to suggest that manipulation from the lingual aspect results in unnecessary lingual nerve morbidity. Bone and tooth removal should be from a buccal approach.
